title: It's not a matter of time, it's a matter of timing
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien takes on the common objection that senior secondary classes have no time for explicit teaching, checks for understanding or gradual release. His central move is to relocate the problem: it is not a shortage of time but poor timing, caused by badly sequenced lessons and too much class time given to independent practice. He argues that explicitly taught lessons only look slower, because they secure understanding before moving on and so avoid re-teaching misconceptions later. He draws on his own senior classes, which finish assessments by mid to late August and keep weeks free for targeted revision. He adds that senior students are still novices in a subject and have the same working-memory limits as younger ones, so chunking, rehearsal and scaffold fading remain essential. The post closes by framing slow, deliberate teaching as an investment that pays back many times over.
points: Teachers who say there is no time for explicit teaching in senior years usually have a planning and sequencing problem, plus too much independent practice, rather than a real time shortage.
Flipped-classroom style independent work in class produces Coe's poor proxies for learning, letting misconceptions harden into long-term memory unnoticed.
Explicit lessons look slower but are faster overall because checking for understanding prevents the re-teaching that follows rushed coverage.
Senior students are relative novices with the same working-memory limits as juniors, so chunking and gradual release (not a sheer cliff to independence) still apply.
The practical payoff of the author's approach is early completion of school-based assessment and weeks of targeted exam revision.
quotes: The issue of time seems to rear its ugly head for two main reasons which I have noticed over (for lack of a better word) time. Poor planning/sequencing of lessons and too much time allocated to independent practice.

This often leads to one of Robert Coe’s Poor Proxies for Learning where students look engaged or busy but the teacher will often have no idea what the students know or what misconceptions have developed because they have been left to learn it themselves. Furthermore, by the time the misconception is caught it may be too late as the student has had time to practice that misconception into permanence in their long term memory through this process.

Interestingly, to an outside observer it may look as if an explicitly taught lesson is actually moving slower than other methods as it may take a full hour to deliver a single key knowledge point, sometimes even longer. However, this is due to the nature of ensuring student success before moving on. The Science of Learning acknowledges that learning is sequential and cumulative and therefore without stopping down to check for understanding, moving on ahead may be faster but could be a futile effort.

The problem this creates is that students may again learn and practice a misconception or have no conceptual understanding of the knowledge in the first place. This is going to mean that when it comes to revision programs or spaced retrieval, it is likely the teacher is going to need to re-teach the content almost from the base level because enough time will have passed that the students have forgotten the majority of it.

A final reason why senior students also need the Science of Learning embedded in their classes is that working memory still has the same limits in a senior classroom as a junior classroom. Just because those students are older does not mean that their brains are any more or less capable of holding more than a few novel items at a time.

So many senior classrooms essentially deliver all of the knowledge all in one batch and then expect students to be able to respond to questions based on it all. This is essentially like giving students 2 balls to hold, and then continuing to pass them more and more while still expecting them to hold on to all of them. Eventually the balls are going to drop.

There are on average 23 hours a day where you do not have control over what those students are learning, so make that time worth something. It may take a little bit more time now, both in planning and teaching but that time is an investment and it is going to mature ten-fold.
